3.text: do not differ very much from the Chukchee. During my stay on the Kolyma,

4.text: I brought back from the Large Anui River the ancient dress of a Yukaghir

5.text: shaman, along with his drum and other appurtenances. About this time a

6.text: well-to-do merchant, Nekhoroshev, who had come from Yakutsk a few years

7.text: before, suddenly had an attack of some mental disease. His wife invited a

8.text: Yakut shaman to practise some magic for his recovery. The shaman declared

9.text: that he wanted to use my shamanistic dress. The woman, afraid of the

10.text: consequences, applied to the priest of Sredne-Kolymsk, who performed the

11.text: duties of superintendent. He said with great prudence, “If it can be of any

12.text: use, I permit you to use both the shaman and the dress.” A few years

13.text: afterwards, in 1902, a large sum of money (28,000 rubles) was spirited away

14.text: from the Board of Police of the Kolyma. After some ineffectual searching,

15.text: the chief officer, acting on the advice of the same superintendent of the church,

16.text: applied to shamans. At first a Yakut shaman was invited, then a Tungus

17.text: shaman; but both proved to be more sober-minded than the members of the

18.text: Administration. They declared that the paper moneys of the Government

19.text: have water-marks in their tissue, so their assistant spirits cannot look for them.

20.text: Two years after that it appeared that the money was stolen by the sacristan

21.text: of the church. These two episodes may give an idea of the actual state of

22.text: Christianity among the Russian creoles on the Kolyma.

23.text: AMERICAN INFLUENCE. — The Maritime Chukchee keep almost wholly

24.text: beyond the reach of Russian influence. Instead of that, on the Pacific shore,

25.text: chiefly in the Eskimo villages, American influence is felt in some degree.

26.text: This influence has come about through trade with the whalers. I have spoken

27.text: of it before. After half a century of commercial intercourse with American

28.text: whalers, not a few of the younger people speak some English. They have

29.text: learned civilized methods of counting, the use of the calendar, of watches,

30.text: and of the ship’s compass. Some of them are employed on whaling-ships

31.text: as extra hands, being good seamen. Occasionally they visit Cape Nome,

32.text: St. Michaels, and even San Francisco. When I was at Indian Point, some

33.text: of my younger native friends expressed a warm desire to learn reading and

34.text: writing. One of them, Čeˊlqar by name, had succeeded by his own efforts

35.text: in telling the letters of the alphabet when printed in large type. I have

36.text: a letter of his, written in large printed characters, with barbarous spelling

37.text: curiously phonetic. The letter runs as follows: “I WLTL YUO ALASNEIT

38.text: ME CAM POORESSEB ME NO KERDT NETD. MERAKN MAN.

39.text: NOO . GOOD . MAI POOI. CEREI AYN PEIEB E LIKM ROOSEN
